headline: A Diffie-Hellman key proves possession by agreeing a secret with the authority, without signing anything.
summary: RFC 4211 gives a key agreement key four ways to prove possession, and the fourth needs no signature: the requester and the authority agree a secret, and that secret keys a MAC over the request. pki.crmf.build assembles it, which is the last of the four it did not. Section 4.3 requires every Diffie-Hellman implementation to support this proof.

Added: pki.crmf.build assembles the agreeMAC proof of possession (RFC 4211 section 4.3, RFC 2875 section 3). The requester supplies pop.key, its own Diffie-Hellman private key, and pop.caCert, the authority's certificate it already holds; the two agree a secret, a key is derived from it, and that key MACs the request. The proof carries id-dhPop-static-HMAC-SHA1, and both that OID and id-alg-dhPOP are registered.

The proof value is the DhPopStatic structure section 3 defines, not the bare MAC: the BIT STRING carries a SEQUENCE of the issuer name and serial number of the certificate the authority's key came from, and the HMAC result as an OCTET STRING. The section says so after the computation it describes, "i.e. encodes the above sequence instead of the raw output from 3d".

The key is derived as RFC 2875 section 3 states it: SHA-1 over the authority certificate's subject name, the agreed secret, and its issuer name, in that order. Section 4.3 settles which certificate those names come from and what to do when one is absent, so an authority certificate whose subject name is empty contributes its subjectAltName instead, and one carrying neither is refused rather than keyed from nothing. That alternative name is read as the GeneralNames it is rather than measured, since the certificate parser surfaces an extension's bytes without running the decoder registered for it: an empty list carries a length while naming nobody, and so does one holding a value that no arm of the GeneralName choice covers. Section 4.3 states the same fallback for an empty issuer name, which a certificate reaching this proof cannot carry: RFC 5280 section 4.1.2.4 requires a non-empty issuer, and the certificate parser enforces it.

The MAC covers the DER certReq, and the request must name both a subject and a public key. Section 4.3's own ASN.1 comment states both, where the prose states neither: the proof is "a MAC (over the DER-encoded value of the certReq parameter in CertReqMsg, which must include both subject and publicKey)". A template naming only one of them is refused.

pop.key must be the private half of certTemplate.publicKey. The authority derives its side of the agreement from the requested key, so a private key from another pair agrees a secret with the authority and yields a MAC the authority cannot reproduce: a proof of possession of something the request never asked to have certified. The encryptedKey arm holds its enclosed key to the same rule.

The proof is admitted only for a finite-field Diffie-Hellman pair, which is what section 3 defines it over, and only when the requester's key can actually reach the authority's, which section 4.3 requires. An elliptic-curve or montgomery pair agrees a secret through the same operation and is refused rather than emitted under an OID naming something the recipient is not performing; so is a key on another group, and a key this runtime cannot classify is named as unrecognized rather than reported as a key type. Every copy of private material the proof allocates is cleared before the call returns, on the refusing paths as well as the building one: the agreed secret, the key derived from it, and the copy taken of the caller's key. The caller's own key is left untouched.

The authority certificate is read in both encodings a finite-field key is written in. An X.509 Diffie-Hellman certificate names dhpublicnumber and carries X9.42 DomainParameters (RFC 3279 section 2.3.3) where this runtime classifies only the PKCS#3 form, so such a key is rewritten into the form it reads. The request still carries the encoding the caller asked to have certified.

The group an authority certificate states is checked before a secret is agreed in it, in either encoding. Whether a set of parameters describes the key it carries is asked of every key read, since a request carries those parameters to whoever reads it next: the order must divide p-1, be an order the generator has, be prime, and hold the public value, and the cofactor must match. The floors are the strength the agreement itself needs, and only a key being agreed with is held to them, so the encryptedKey arm, which sends a private key to be archived and agrees nothing, still enrolls a legacy group. The modulus must be prime. Where the certificate states a subgroup order, that order must divide p-1, must be an order the generator actually has, must be prime, and must be large enough to hide an exponent: a prime order makes the public value's order exactly that value rather than a divisor of it, which is worth nothing when the value is small, and three is prime. Where the certificate states no order, which the PKCS#3 form cannot, the modulus must be a safe prime, whose element orders are one, two, r and 2r alone; that bounds the order to (p-1)/2, so the same floor applies there, since seven is a safe prime whose own subgroup has order three. The public value must lie inside the group, and inside the stated subgroup where there is one. The floor is the smallest subgroup order NIST SP 800-56A states for a finite-field group. The modulus carries a floor of its own, of 2048 bits, which is the size the toolkit's linter already names for a public key: a large subgroup says a value is hard to take a discrete log of inside the group and says nothing about the group itself, and a 512-bit safe prime has a 255-bit subgroup while the secret agreed in it is recoverable. An authority certificate on a smaller group is refused, so a 1024-bit legacy group no longer completes this proof. These proofs run on each build and their cost grows with the modulus, from a fraction of a second over a 2048-bit group to a second or two at the 4096-bit bound.

The parameters are sized before anything is computed with them, since these tests raise one operand to the power of another and prove a modulus prime, while the DER reader admits an integer far wider than any Diffie-Hellman group. The bound is 4096 bits, which covers every MODP group a certificate carries. Every container is read for the tag it carries rather than for having children, so a context-specific constructed value in place of the DomainParameters SEQUENCE is refused rather than rewritten into a key that imports while the request carries the original. The cofactor and the validation parameters are each optional and independent, so a fourth field is read by its tag: the cofactor is held against p and q, and the validation parameters against the seed BIT STRING and pgenCounter INTEGER they consist of. The public key BIT STRING must hold whole octets, since the codec admits a nonzero unused-bit count whose padding bits are zero and that BIT STRING is carried through unchanged.

The authority certificate's keyUsage is enforced. A keyUsage extension restricts the certified key to the purposes it asserts (RFC 5280 section 4.2.1.3), and this proof uses the authority's key to agree a secret, so a certificate that states its purposes without stating keyAgreement is refused rather than used for it. A certificate carrying no keyUsage states no restriction and is unaffected.
Fixed: pki.sigstore.verifyBundle refuses a bundle that carries both content arms. A bundle setting dsse_envelope and message_signature together was verified on the envelope alone, returning a verdict that said nothing about the other arm the bundle carried. The bundle's content is a oneof, so exactly one arm may be present and both is now sigstore/bad-bundle.

The same rule holds for verificationMaterial, whose certificate, x509CertificateChain and publicKey are a oneof of the same kind. More than one arm set drew the leaf certificate from one and the chain it is validated through from another, so the certificate whose key was checked and the certificates it was checked through came from different statements about the same signer, and a publicKey beside either certificate arm named a second signer identity the verdict said nothing about.
